answer_text:
Over \(\mathbb{C}\), every \(6\times 6\) matrix is similar (conjugate) to a Jordan canonical form.  
The characteristic polynomial is

\[
(x-5)^6,
\]

so the only eigenvalue is \(5\), with algebraic multiplicity \(6\). Thus every such matrix has Jordan form consisting of Jordan blocks \(J_k(5)\) whose sizes sum to \(6\).

Two matrices are conjugate over \(\mathbb{C}\) exactly when they have the same Jordan block sizes. Therefore, the conjugacy classes are in bijection with integer partitions of \(6\).

The partitions of \(6\) are:

\[
\begin{aligned}
&1+1+1+1+1+1,\\
&2+1+1+1+1,\\
&2+2+1+1,\\
&2+2+2,\\
&3+1+1+1,\\
&3+2+1,\\
&3+3,\\
&4+1+1,\\
&4+2,\\
&5+1,\\
&6.
\end{aligned}
\]

There are \(11\) conjugacy classes total.

The diagonalizable matrix

\[
D=\begin{pmatrix}
5&0&0&0&0&0\\
0&5&0&0&0&0\\
0&0&5&0&0&0\\
0&0&0&5&0&0\\
0&0&0&0&5&0\\
0&0&0&0&0&5
\end{pmatrix}
\]

corresponds to the partition

\[
1+1+1+1+1+1.
\]

The question asks for matrices that are **not** diagonalizable to \(D\), so we exclude this one case. Hence the number of remaining conjugacy classes is

\[
11-1=10.
\]

\[
\boxed{10}
\]
